sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Establishes the rationale and origin of the FHWA dual-criterion classification system (philosophy of behavior plus method of grouting), first introduced in the FHWA State-of-Practice Review (1997) and refined since. The system enables clear communication among designers, contractors, and owners, and lets engineers specify micropiles by both design intent and construction methodology. Classification structure for the chapter is set up here and detailed in Sections 2.2 and 2.3.
sections.body: A rational classification system for micropiles is essential for communication among designers, contractors, and owners. The FHWA classification system presented in this chapter categorizes micropiles according to two criteria: (1) the philosophy of behavior (i.e., how the micropile is intended to function within the foundation system), and (2) the method of grouting used during construction. This dual classification enables engineers to specify micropiles based on both the design intent and the construction methodology. The classification system was first introduced in the FHWA State-of-Practice Review (1997) and has been refined based on subsequent experience and research.
key_points: FHWA classification uses two independent criteria: behavior philosophy and grouting method
Essential for clear communication among designers, contractors, and owners
Originally introduced in FHWA State-of-Practice Review (1997)
Refined based on subsequent research and field experience
sections.applicability: Framework for classifying micropile applications and grouting methods in design specifications.

sections.title: Classification by Philosophy of Behavior
sections.summary: Classification by intended function: CASE 1 micropiles are directly loaded individual structural members (or small connected groups) acting like conventional deep foundation elements, used for new structure support, underpinning, seismic retrofit, and scour protection - the most common US application. CASE 2 micropiles are reticulated networks that reinforce a soil mass to form an in-situ composite, used for slope stabilization, earth retention, and settlement reduction - common in Europe but less so in the US. The CASE classification determines which design chapter (5 or 6) governs.
sections.body: Micropiles are classified by their intended function within the foundation system as either CASE 1 or CASE 2 elements. CASE 1 micropiles are loaded directly, either axially or laterally, and are designed to resist the applied loads as individual structural members or as a small group of elements connected by a pile cap. CASE 1 micropiles function in a manner similar to conventional deep foundation elements. CASE 1 is the most common micropile application in the United States and includes: (a) support of new structures, (b) underpinning of existing structures (e.g., settlement mitigation, increased loading), (c) seismic retrofit of existing foundations, and (d) scour protection for existing bridge foundations. CASE 2 micropiles are used as a reticulated network of elements to reinforce the ground, creating an in-situ reinforced soil composite. Unlike CASE 1 where individual elements carry specific loads, CASE 2 relies on the interaction between the micropiles and the surrounding soil mass. CASE 2 applications include: (a) slope stabilization, (b) earth retention, and (c) settlement reduction in soft ground. CASE 2 applications are less common in the US but have been used extensively in Europe.
key_points: CASE 1: Directly loaded elements functioning as individual structural members or small groups
CASE 1 applications: new foundations, underpinning, seismic retrofit, scour protection
CASE 1 is the most common micropile application in the US
CASE 2: Reticulated network reinforcing the soil mass as an in-situ composite
CASE 2 applications: slope stabilization, earth retention, settlement reduction
CASE 2 relies on micropile-soil interaction rather than individual element capacity
CASE 2 is more common in European practice

sections.title: Classification by Method of Grouting
sections.summary: Classification by grouting method, the dominant control on grout-to-ground bond capacity. Type A places neat cement grout by gravity tremie only (lowest bond, used in rock and stiff/hard cohesive soils). Type B injects grout under pressure of 0.5 to 1.0 MPa as temporary casing is withdrawn (most common in US, effective in granular and soft-to-stiff cohesive soils). Type C uses a primary gravity grout followed by one secondary pressurized injection above 1.0 MPa through a grout tube (predominantly French practice). Type D uses multiple injections through a tube-a-manchette at 2 to 8 MPa to fracture the surrounding ground and grout body, achieving the highest bond values (European practice).
sections.body: The second criterion for micropile classification is the method of grouting, which significantly influences the grout-to-ground bond capacity and therefore the geotechnical resistance of the micropile. Four types are defined: Type A micropiles use gravity grout only, where neat cement grout is placed under gravity head through tremie methods. Type A micropiles achieve the lowest grout-to-ground bond values and are most commonly used in rock or very stiff/hard cohesive soils. Type B micropiles use pressure grouting where grout is injected into the drill hole as temporary steel casing is withdrawn. Typical grouting pressures range from 0.5 to 1.0 MPa, which enhances the grout-to-ground bond along the bond zone. Type B is the most common micropile grouting method in US practice. Type C micropiles use a two-step process: (1) primary neat cement grout is placed under gravity head, then (2) before the primary grout hardens, a single injection of additional grout is made through a grout tube (tube-a-manchette or similar) at pressures typically exceeding 1.0 MPa. Type C grouting is used primarily in French practice. Type D micropiles also use a two-step process similar to Type C, but multiple injections of grout are made through a tube-a-manchette (also known as a sleeve port pipe), with each injection targeted at specific intervals along the bond zone at pressures of 2 to 8 MPa. Type D grouting achieves the highest grout-to-ground bond values. Type D is used primarily in European practice and is less common in the US.
key_points: Type A: Gravity grout only; lowest bond values; best in rock or very stiff cohesive soils
Type B: Pressure grouting during casing withdrawal at 0.5-1.0 MPa; most common in US
Type C: Gravity grout followed by one pressure injection at >1.0 MPa; French practice
Type D: Gravity grout followed by multiple injections via tube-a-manchette at 2-8 MPa; highest bond
Grouting method directly controls grout-to-ground bond capacity
Bond strength increases from Type A through Type D
Type B is the most common grouting method in US transportation practice

sections.title: Micropile Classification Summary
sections.summary: Combines CASE (1 or 2) and Type (A, B, C, or D) into the complete FHWA classification matrix shown in Table 2-1, with eight possible combinations. CASE 1 Type B is the most common in US practice. The CASE classification points the designer to Chapter 5 (structure foundations) or Chapter 6 (slope stabilization), while the Type classification controls which presumptive grout-to-ground bond values from Table 5-3 are used for geotechnical capacity calculations. In practice, the designer specifies required bond values and the contractor selects the Type that will reliably achieve them on the site.
sections.body: Table 2-1 summarizes the complete FHWA micropile classification system combining both the philosophy of behavior (CASE 1 or CASE 2) and the method of grouting (Type A, B, C, or D). Any combination of CASE and Type is possible, resulting in eight potential classifications (e.g., CASE 1, Type B is the most common combination in US practice). For design purposes, the CASE classification determines the design methodology to be used (Chapter 5 for CASE 1, Chapter 6 for CASE 2), while the Type classification determines the grout-to-ground bond values used for geotechnical capacity calculations (Table 5-3). In practice, the designer should specify the design loads and the minimum required grout-to-ground bond values, while the contractor selects the specific grouting method (Type) that will reliably achieve the required bond values for the site-specific ground conditions.
key_points: Eight possible classifications combining CASE (1 or 2) with Type (A, B, C, or D)
CASE 1, Type B is the most common combination in US practice
CASE classification determines the design methodology (Chapter 5 or 6)
Type classification determines grout-to-ground bond values (Table 5-3)
Designer specifies design loads and minimum bond values
